title: Load balancing
subtitle: One server is a starting point, not a scaling plan.
question: If you double service replicas, will end-to-end latency halve?
explanation: Replicas share service work. They cannot remove a downstream database bottleneck. Compare utilization and tail latency with the same seed, and remember that this model assumes independent exponential service times.
challenge: Run at least two service replicas and keep modeled errors at or below 5%.

title: Caching
subtitle: The fastest database request is the one you avoid.
question: Which database requests still happen when the read-cache hit ratio reaches 90%?
explanation: A read hit completes at the cache; a miss continues to the database. Writes always continue downstream. Hit ratio is an explicit assumption, not a modeled eviction policy. A cache is not a substitute for durable storage.
challenge: Use at least 80% read hits and show database visits below half of generated requests, with at most 5% errors.

title: Database replication
subtitle: More readers. The same write bottleneck.
question: Will adding read replicas also increase write capacity?
explanation: This simplified model separates read and primary-write pools. Read replicas add read capacity only. Replication lag, consistency and failover are deliberately omitted; do not infer availability from the replica slider.
challenge: Use two or more database read-pool replicas with at most 5% modeled errors.

title: Queues and backpressure
subtitle: A queue buys time. Workers supply capacity.
question: What happens to queue depth when arrivals exceed worker capacity?
explanation: A finite FIFO queue absorbs a burst but eventually fills. Adding independent workers can drain it faster. This lesson models queue workers as a processing stage before the database, not durable message delivery guarantees.
challenge: Observe a nonzero worker queue while completing the run with at most 5% errors.

title: Rate limiting
subtitle: Protect the system before the system protects itself.
question: Is a policy rejection the same as an application failure?
explanation: A token bucket allows a bounded burst, then admits work at the configured rate. Rejections are reported separately from service errors. Choosing a rate is a product trade-off: fewer admitted requests can protect downstream latency.
challenge: Trigger policy rejections while keeping service errors at zero.
